I've gathered substantial material from the main commentary sources. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes.

---

## Isaiah 17 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview

This chapter is titled "The Burden against Damascus" (or "oracle concerning Damascus"). Damascus was the capital of Syria (Aram), which had formed an anti-Assyrian alliance with the northern kingdom of Israel (Ephraim). The two had also conspired against Judah (Isaiah 7). Most commentators agree the chapter addresses both Syria and Israel together because of this alliance. Assyria destroyed Damascus in 732 BC and Samaria in 722 BC, fulfilling the prophecy in its near-term sense. The chapter closes (vv. 12–14) with a sudden oracle against the raging nations that God will rebuke and scatter — widely applied to the Assyrian army under Sennacherib and, by extension, to all who plunder God's people.

---

### v. 1 — "This is the burden against Damascus: 'Behold, Damascus is no longer a city; it has become a heap of ruins.'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Gill:** "A heavy and grievous prophecy." Damascus was a very ancient city (Gen 15:2), head of the Syrian kingdom. It was destroyed by Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:9), later by Nebuchadnezzar (Jer 49:24), yet rebuilt again and still existed in the Apostle Paul's time (Acts 9:22; 2 Cor 11:32). The "behold" signals something remarkable and unexpected.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Ellicott:** The words emphasise the result of the Assyrian invasion. Damascus, "the city of ancient days" (Gen 15:2), would lose its glory and be "struck out, as it were, from the list of the great cities of the world." Writing probably early in Hezekiah's reign, Isaiah looks forward to a further fulfilment beyond the partial one recorded in 2 Kings 16:9.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Damascus has been destroyed oftener than any other town but has a wonderful power of rising again. The destruction by Sargon (c. 720 BC) is probably intended here.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html

**Modern Scholarship:**
- **Peake's Commentary:** Dates the oracle between 736–735 BC, before the Syro-Ephraimite invasion of Judah, since that invasion is not mentioned. Damascus fell in 732 BC.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/isaiah-17.html

---

### v. 2 — "The cities of Aroer are forsaken; they will be left to the flocks, which will lie down with no one to fear."

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** Notes there were two cities named Aroer — one in Reuben (Deut 2:36), one in Gad near Rabbah of Ammon (Num 32:34). But this passage suggests a more northern location, in closer connection with Damascus. Possibly the latter Aroer had allied with Damascus and shared its fate. The name "Aroer" means "laid bare," ominously fitting. The picture of flocks lying undisturbed in city streets echoes the desolation imagery of Babylon in Isaiah 13:21.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Identifies this Aroer with the "Gal'gar" (Gargar) of Sargon's annals — a city united in league with Damascus, Samaria, Arpad, and Simyra. Sargon besieged, took, and reduced it to ashes. Flocks pastured on city sites marked "the very extreme of desolation."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html
- **Gill:** The cities become so depopulated that sheep — naturally timid creatures — lie down with "none to make them afraid," because no human remains to disturb them.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm

---

### v. 3 — "The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the sovereignty from Damascus. The remnant of Aram will be like the splendor of the Israelites,' declares the LORD of Hosts."

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** The alliance of the two kingdoms is prominent in Isaiah's thoughts. Both shall fall together. With "stern, grave irony," the downfall of "the remnant of Syria" is painted: it shall be "as the glory of the children of Israel" — i.e., fleeting and transient, as Israel's glory had proved to be. Notes a possible reference to Hosea 9:11, "Ephraim, their glory shall fly away like a bird."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Gill:** "The fortress" is Samaria, the metropolis of Ephraim/the ten tribes, destroyed by Shalmaneser (2 Kings 17:6). Syria, which had been in alliance with Israel, would share the same fate. Both would be stripped of their grandeur and wealth.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Sargon did not destroy Samaria on his first capture (722 BC) but reduced it to a heap of ruins on its second capture. The kingdom from Damascus: after Rezin was slain by Tiglath-Pileser (c. 732 BC), Damascus reasserted independence in 721 BC, but in 720 BC was reduced and destroyed. The phrase "remnant of Syria" shows Syria was already but a remnant from Tiglath-Pileser's earlier blow; now she would cease to exist. The line "they shall be as the glory of the children of Israel" is **ironical**, made apparent by v. 4.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html

**Differing Nuance:**
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Sees the irony as pointing to Israel's (Ephraim's) own coming loss of glory. Syria's remnant will share the same fate as Israel's fading glory — both will be humbled together.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-17/

---

### v. 4 — "'In that day the splendor of Jacob will fade, and the fat of his body will waste away,'"

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** "Jacob" stands, as commonly in the prophets, for the northern kingdom (Israel). The "glory" becoming "thin" and "fatness waxing lean" points to the downfall, or "emaciation," of that kingdom. The word rendered "made thin" is the same as "impoverished" in Judges 6:8.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Gill:** Israel's glory lay in the superior number of their tribes to Judah, their multitude of cities and inhabitants. Now they would be thinned by vast numbers being carried captive. Their wealth and riches would be taken away — like a man in a consumption reduced to skin and bones.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Constable:** In the day of God's judgment, Jacob's prosperity would become lean, as when one grows old and loses his former strength, "because of her unbelief: her lack of trust in God."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-17.html

---

### v. 5 — "as the reaper gathers the standing grain and harvests the ears with his arm, as one gleans heads of grain in the Valley of Rephaim."

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** The conqueror shall plunder the cities of Israel as the reaper cuts off ears of corn. With "Dantesque vividness" the prophet localises the imagery: the Valley of Rephaim ("of the giants") lay south-west of Jerusalem, famous for its fertility and often attacked by Philistines who came to carry off its crops (2 Sam 23:13). The prophet had seen the reaper's work and saw in it a parable of the Assyrian invader's work.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Gill:** Israel was like a field of standing corn for number, beauty, and glory. The Assyrian was the harvestman, cutting them down with ease and quick dispatch — they were no more able to stand before him than corn before the reaper. The Valley of Rephaim was a very fruitful place where ears of corn were large and heavy, so gleaning was done with great care.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Death is the "harvestman" here, gathering Israelites into his garner. "Ears" only were reaped — the stalk cut close under the ear, as was the practice also in Egypt.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html

---

### v. 6 — "'Yet gleanings will remain, like an olive tree that has been beaten — two or three berries atop the tree, four or five on its fruitful branches,' declares the LORD, the God of Israel."

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** The idea of the "remnant" persists, even for the northern kingdom. First the vineyard, then the olive-yard supplies a similitude. The "shaking" (or beating) followed on the beating of Deut 24:20. Even after beating, a few berries remain on the topmost bough — inaccessible to the gatherer's hand or staff.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Gill:** A remnant according to the election of grace would be preserved among the ten tribes — as few as two or three berries at the top, four or five on fruitful branches. The Targum paraphrases: "so shall the righteous be left alone in the world among the kingdoms."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Corrects the KJV's "gleaning grapes" — the gleaning intended is of an olive-ground, not a vineyard. The olive crop was obtained by beating the trees (Deut 24:20). The owner was forbidden to "go over the boughs again," so that a portion remained for the stranger, widow, and fatherless.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Emphasises that God's judgment, though severe, always leaves a remnant. God's mercy appears even in judgment.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-17/

---

### v. 7 — "In that day men will look to their Maker and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel."

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** These are "words of warning hardly less than of promise." There will be a return to the true faith of Israel, but that return is brought about by bitter experience of the results of idolatry. In the hour of calamity, men's eyes will turn to "the Holy One of Israel."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Gill:** The remnant according to the election of grace shall look to God for help, supply, support, and protection — and particularly to Christ, who is the Maker of all things, for all spiritual blessings. They shall look to "the Holy One of Israel" who is the Redeemer (Isa 43:14). The Targum reads: "his eyes shall hope for the Word of the Holy One of Israel."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** In the midst of severe judgment, some will respond as they should — with humble respect for God. One of God's purposes in judgment is to turn focus away from idols toward Him.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-17/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Provides historical evidence: in Josiah's reign, offerings were made for the temple service by men of "Manasseh and Ephraim, and of all the remnant of Israel" (2 Chron 34:9), showing this revulsion of feeling.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html

**Differing Views — Who is the "man"?**
- Most traditional commentators (Gill, Ellicott, Guzik) apply this to the faithful remnant of Israel.
- **Constable** extends it also to "the Arameans (Syrians)" — the coming destruction would cause both Israelites and Syrians to turn to their Maker.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-17.html
- **Peake's Commentary** considers vv. 7–8 "an insertion" — a later addition asserting the effect of judgment, breaking the flow of the original oracle.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/isaiah-17.html

---

### v. 8 — "They will not look to the altars they have fashioned with their hands or to the Asherahs and incense altars they have made with their fingers."

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** "The groves or the images" — literally, the *Asherah* or the *sun-images*. The former were conical, tree-like pillars symbolising worship of a Canaanite goddess, the giver of good fortune. The "images" are *sun-images*, emblems of Baal — probably pillars or conical stones common in Phoenician worship.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Gill:** The repentant man will not look to his own good works as altars to atone for sin, nor to idols. "Good men will not look to their own works, what their fingers have wrought, as groves to shelter them from divine wrath … but reject them, and look to Christ only."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The altars at Dan and Bethel (1 Kings 12:28–33) may be intended, or additional idolatrous altars (2 Kings 17:11; Hosea 8:11). Josiah later broke down altars throughout all the land of Israel, apparently with the consent of the inhabitants.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** God's judgment strips away every wrong thing trusted in — pagan altars, wooden images, incense altars. "Their only hope was in the LORD."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-17/

---

### v. 9 — "In that day their strong cities will be like forsaken thickets and summits, abandoned to the Israelites and to utter desolation."

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** Better translated: "his fortified cities shall be like a forsaken tract of forest and hill-top." These were the usual sites of fortresses (2 Chron 27:4). They shall be left uninhabited and in ruins. The LXX paraphrases: "thy cities shall be forsaken, like as the Amorites and Hivites forsook them before the face of the children of Israel." The whole verse recalls "the great forsaking" of Isaiah 6:12.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The reference is to the condition of the land when it passed out of Canaanite possession — then forsaken and desolate. So shall it be once more when Israel is expelled for the same sins (2 Kings 17:7–8).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html
- **Gill:** The strong cities of Ephraim/Jacob would be forsaken of their inhabitants, like a bough stripped of its leaves or a dead, dry uppermost branch with nothing on it. The same cities the Canaanites left for fear of the Israelites, the Israelites would now leave for fear of the Assyrians.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Jerome (cited by Gill):** Applied the whole to the cities of Judea being forsaken when the Romans besieged Jerusalem — a calamity coming for their "neglect and forgetfulness of Jesus the Saviour."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm

---

### v. 10 — "For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and failed to remember the Rock of your refuge. Therefore, though you cultivate delightful plots and set out cuttings from exotic vines—"

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** "The Rock of thy strength" — Jehovah as the true defence, the fortress rock (Deut 32:4), is contrasted with the rock-fortresses in which the people had put their trust. "Therefore shalt thou plant pleasant plants" — better, "thou didst plant." The word for "pleasant" (*Naaman*) is found only here as a common noun; it appears as a proper name in Gen 46:21 and in "Naaman the Syrian" (2 Kings 5:1). The prophet chose this term to indicate the foreign, specifically Syrian, character of the worship Israel had adopted. Cheyne connects it with the "gardens of Adonis" — fair but perishable (Plato, *Phaedrus* 276 B). The "strange slips" are literally "vine-slips of a strange one" — i.e., of a strange god (cf. Jer 2:21).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Gill:** Israel forgot the God who had been the author of their salvation in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in many instances since. They were not mindful of "the rock of thy strength" — their strong Rock who had supplied, supported, protected, and defended them. The "pleasant plants" and "strange slips" refer not only to literal horticulture but to false and foreign doctrines inculcating idolatry and superstition, which are "pleasing to the flesh."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** The sin of forgetting God "may not seem great on the surface, but it's devastating because He is the God of our salvation — if we forget Him, we forget about our salvation itself." Satan does not need to make us bank robbers or murderers; it is enough to make us simply forget. Citing Calvin: "We are thus reminded that we ought not to be so impatient in enduring chastisements, which cure us of the fearfully dangerous disease of apostasy."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-17/
- **Constable:** The description of cultivating plants represents "a pagan custom designed to secure the favor of local gods." Rather than trusting in their saving God, the Israelites had planted "little seedlings of faith in idols."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-17.html

**Modern Scholarship:**
- **Peake's Commentary:** Confirms the "Adonis gardens" reading. Adonis (Tammuz, Ezek 8:14) was a vegetation deity. His worship involved pots or baskets of earth sown with flowers, stimulated to rapid growth, then quickly withered — symbolising the death of vegetation in autumn. The prophet uses this as a metaphor: Israel, in its alliance with Syria, had adopted this Syrian cult, and its plans and hopes would be just as quickly crushed.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/isaiah-17.html

---

### v. 11 — "though on the day you plant you make them grow, and on that morning you help your seed sprout — yet the harvest will vanish on the day of disease and incurable pain."

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** "Thou makest, or, thou fencest, thy plant." The alliance between Syria and Ephraim is compared in the rapidity of its growth with the "gardens of Adonis." All the "harvest heaps" from such planting end not in harvest joy (Isa 9:3) but in "grief and incurable pain."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Gill:** All means and methods would be used to make the plant grow, with diligence and early care, and with seeming promising success — "and yet all should be in vain, and to no purpose." Just when the fruit was ripe and about to be gathered, the enemy would come and take it all away. Instead of harvest joy, there would be "desperate sorrow" and "deadly" grief, leaving them without hope.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** One aspect of the LORD's judgment is bringing hard work to nothing. They will work hard to plant and grow crops (both literally and figuratively), but the harvest will be "a heap of ruins." Compares with Haggai 1:6 ("You have sown much, and bring in little"). "How much better it is to be listening to Jesus and to have our service directed and blessed by Him (Luke 5:1–10)."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-17/
- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** "National repentance may come too late to avert national ruin." The crisis of a nation's fate is brought on by slow degrees. A remnant may save their own souls, but they cannot save their country.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html

---

### v. 12 — "Alas, the tumult of many peoples; they rage like the roaring seas and clamoring nations; they rumble like the crashing of mighty waters."

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** These three verses (12–14) stand as "an isolated fragment," probably placed here because it begins like Isaiah 18:1. It may have been connected with the progress of Sennacherib's army. The "rushing of mighty waters" to describe an army's march parallels Isaiah 8:7–8.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Rather, Ho for the tumult of many peoples!" The advance of an army composed of soldiers from many nations is descried — a tumult compared with "seas that are tumultuous." Under the circumstances of the time, it is "reasonable to suppose the Assyrians to be intended" (cf. Isa 22:6–7).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html
- **Gill:** A new subject begins. The "multitude of many people" is the Assyrian army under Sennacherib, consisting of people of many nations. The noise refers both to the march of the vast army and to the hectoring, blasphemous speeches of Sennacherib and Rabshakeh.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **JFB:** "Ho (Hark)! a noise of," etc. The prophet in vision perceives the vast and mixed Assyrian hosts. The connection with what precedes: notwithstanding the calamities coming on Israel, the people of God shall not be utterly destroyed; the Assyrian spoilers shall perish.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/17.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** God will use other nations to bring judgment against Syria and Israel. They will come "like a flash flood that can't be stopped."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-17/

---

### v. 13 — "The nations rage like the rush of many waters. He rebukes them, and they flee far away, driven before the wind like chaff on the hills, like tumbleweeds before a gale."

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** "But God shall rebuke them" — better, "He shall rebuke them." The insertion of "God" weakens the "sublime indefiniteness of the Hebrew." "Like a rolling thing" — the Hebrew is the same as the "wheel" of Psalm 83:13, probably referring, like the "chaff of the mountains," to whirling dust-clouds driven from an elevated threshing-floor before the wind (Ps 1:4; 35:5).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Gill:** "But God shall rebuke them" — as He did the waters of the Red Sea (Ps 106:9) and as Christ rebuked the winds and sea (Matt 8:26). The word "God" is not in the text but "rightly supplied," for only He could destroy such an army and work such a salvation. "Chaff of the mountains" — it was usual for Jews to thresh and winnow corn on hills and mountains (2 Chron 3:1). Kings and great men are but dust with God; the higher they exalt themselves, the more exposed they are to His wrath. "Like a rolling thing" — or "like a wheel," any round thing like a wisp of straw or stubble easily rolled along by a strong wind. Jarchi interprets it as the down of the thistle.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The destruction of Sennacherib's army in the night was followed by the hasty flight of the survivors (2 Kings 19:36; Isa 37:37). Herodotus says the Egyptians pursued the army and slew vast numbers (Histories, 2.141).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** When God brings the rush of nations against Israel, it does not mean the nations He uses are exempt from judgment. "God can use one sinner to judge another, and then judge the sinner He just used."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-17/

---

### v. 14 — "In the evening, there is sudden terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us and the lot of those who plunder us."

**Traditional Reading:**
- **Ellicott:** The words, though spoken in general terms, "received a special fulfilment in the destruction of Sennacherib's army" (Isa 37:36). The parallelism with v. 11 may have led to the insertion of this oracle in this place.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm
- **Gill:** "At eveningtide trouble" — or terror and consternation, referring to the terror that fell on the Assyrian army when the angel destroyed 185,000 in one night (2 Kings 19:35). "And before the morning he is not" — Sennacherib and the few who escaped fled to Nineveh. "This is the portion of them that spoil us" — this is what all enemies of God's people may expect, sooner or later.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** "This is a comforting principle: Even in the midst of judgment, God shows mercy. As bad as it was going to be for Israel, it could have been worse. … Israel was not at the mercy of circumstances or their enemies; they were at the mercy of God."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-17/
- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** This passage "seems, more distinctly than any other in the purely prophetical chapters, to point to the miraculous destruction of the host which Sennacherib was about to bring against Jerusalem."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-17.html

**Broader Eschatological Reading:**
- **Constable:** The fact that Isaiah does not name a particular nation "suggests that he had more in mind than just one foe, and a perspective that extended far beyond his own day. Many nations would punish Israel over the years." Chapter 18 describes an eschatological defeat of superpowers.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-17.html
- **Barnes' Notes:** The close of the chapter gives assurance to Judah that no alliance formed against them would be successful — this is the "portion" (the just recompense) of all who spoil God's people.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-17.html

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The available sources did not yield strongly divergent denominational readings on this chapter. Most traditional Protestant commentators read Isaiah 17 along the same broad lines. Some nuances:

- **Baptist (Gill, a Reformed Baptist):** Reads vv. 7–8 Christologically — the "Maker" to whom men look is specifically Christ, "the Word by whom all things were made." Also stresses that good men will not look to their own "good works as altars to atone for sin." Strongly predestinarian in noting the "remnant according to the election of grace." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/17.htm)
- **Charismatic/Pentecostal (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Emphasises practical application — Satan uses distraction and forgetfulness rather than dramatic sins; God's judgment is redemptive in purpose. Focus on God's mercy even in judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-17/)
- **Reformed (Calvin, cited by Guzik):** Stresses that chastisements cure "the fearfully dangerous disease of apostasy." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-17/)
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** More restrained, carefully notes textual variants (LXX readings, Hebrew nuances), and sees vv. 12–14 as an "isolated fragment." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/17.htm)

On the specific identity of the "Adonis gardens" in vv. 10–11, there is broad agreement among the sources consulted that this refers to Syrian fertility cult practices adopted by Israel. No denominational splits were evident.

---

## Other Views

### Modern/Critical Scholarship
- **Peake's Commentary:** Dates the main oracle (vv. 1–11) to c. 736–735 BC, before the Syro-Ephraimite invasion of Judah. Considers vv. 7–8 "an insertion" interrupting the original description of judgment. Identifies the "pleasant plants" and "strange slips" as "plantings of Adonis" and "vine-slips of a strange god" — referring to the rapid-growth ritual gardens that withered quickly. Suggests that vv. 12–14 may be post-exilic (though admits it could be Isaianic, with "many nations" meaning the subject peoples in Assyria's army). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/isaiah-17.html)
- **bible.org (Allen):** Notes the NASB's rendering "vine slips of a strange god" (v. 10), directly linking the horticultural imagery to idolatry. Sees v. 14 as having "no verbal, which would denote emphasis," giving a restorative context. The strophe is parallel to Psalm 2 — YHWH sends the nations to punish His people but also judges those same nations. (https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-17)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings
No results were returned from the searches targeting newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org specifically for Isaiah 17 verse-by-verse commentary. This remains a gap in the research.

## Summary of Key Themes

1. **Judgment on Syria and Israel together** — their anti-God alliance brings shared destruction (vv. 1–6).
2. **The remnant preserved** — God always preserves a small remnant, like the few olives left after beating (v. 6).
3. **Judgment produces repentance** — calamity drives people to look to their Maker and abandon idols (vv. 7–8).
4. **Forgetting God is the root sin** — not dramatic evil, but the quiet neglect of the God of salvation, the Rock of refuge (v. 10).
5. **Human effort without God is futile** — planting, cultivating, and expecting a harvest that never comes (vv. 10–11).
6. **God judges the instruments of His judgment** — the nations He uses to discipline His people are themselves rebuked and scattered like chaff (vv. 12–14).
7. **Comfort for God's people** — "this is the portion of those who plunder us" — God's people are not at the mercy of their enemies but at the mercy of God (v. 14).
